decks.title: Topographical Maps: Grid References, Contours and Heights, Part 1: The grid and contours
goals: Give the four-figure and six-figure grid reference of a feature, eastings first
Name the feature at a given grid reference
Define a contour and find the contour interval of a sheet
Judge steep and gentle slopes from the spacing of contours

slides.heading: Reading a topographical sheet
slides.body_md: A **topographical sheet** is a large-scale map of a small area. It shows relief, rivers, settlements, roads and land use in one picture. In the ICSE map paper you read a real Survey of India sheet. To practise, this chapter uses one **imagined practice sheet** that we built ourselves: it is **not a real place** and it is **not copied from any official sheet**.

rows: Eastings 40 to 50, northings 70 to 80 (100 squares of 1 km)
about 41 m, where the river leaves the sheet

visual.alt: Table of the grid, scale, contour interval and height range of the imagined practice sheet
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: A topographical sheet is a detailed map of a small area. It shows hills, rivers, villages, roads and fields all at once. In the exam you will read a real sheet from the Survey of India. For practice we use one imagined sheet that we built ourselves. It is not a real place, and every answer in this chapter is worked out from its own data.

slides.heading: The grid: eastings and northings
slides.body_md: Grid lines divide the sheet into squares of **1 km by 1 km**; on a printed sheet at 1 cm to 0.5 km each square is **2 cm by 2 cm**. The **vertical lines** are **eastings** and are numbered along the top and bottom edges; the numbers increase towards the east. The **horizontal lines** are **northings**, numbered along the left and right edges; the numbers increase towards the north. Here the eastings run from 40 to 50 and the northings from 70 to 80.

visual.alt: Full imagined practice sheet with grid, contours, drainage, roads, settlements and land use. Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet.
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: Look at the grid first. Vertical lines are called eastings, and their numbers grow as you move east. Horizontal lines are called northings, and their numbers grow as you move north. Each square is one kilometre by one kilometre. On this imagined sheet the eastings run from forty to fifty and the northings from seventy to eighty.

slides.heading: Four-figure grid references
slides.body_md: A **four-figure reference** names one grid square. Rule: read the **easting first** (along the bottom), then the **northing** (up the side), using the two lines that meet at the **south-west (bottom-left) corner** of the square. Remember it as "along the corridor, then up the stairs". The temple lies between easting lines 46 and 47 and between northing lines 74 and 75, so it is in square **4674**.

visual.alt: Extract of the imagined practice sheet showing squares 4673 to 4875 with a temple, a police station, a post office, a well, a river and a canal
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: A four figure reference names a whole square. Always read the easting first, along the bottom, and then the northing, up the side. Use the two lines that meet at the bottom left corner of the square. The temple lies just right of line forty six and just above line seventy four, so it is in square four six seven four.

slides.heading: Six-figure grid references
slides.body_md: To pinpoint a point feature, imagine each side of the square divided into **ten equal parts (tenths, of 0.1 km)**. The six figures are: easting (2 digits) + tenths eastwards (1 digit), then northing (2 digits) + tenths northwards (1 digit). The temple is 3 tenths east of line 46 and 6 tenths north of line 74, so its six-figure reference is **463746**.

visual.alt: Table showing how the six-figure references of a temple, a police station and a well are built from easting, northing and tenths
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: For a point feature we need six figures. Divide each side of the square into ten equal parts. Write the easting number, then how many tenths east of it the feature lies, then the northing number and its tenths. The temple is three tenths east of line forty six and six tenths north of line seventy four, so its reference is four six three seven four six.

slides.heading: Worked example: a reference for the dispensary
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Give the four-figure and the six-figure reference of the dispensary (Dis) in Sonakhedi.

**Step 1.** Find the easting line just west of it: **43**. The dispensary is about 1 tenth east of it (0.15 km).

**Step 2.** Find the northing line just south of it: **72**. It is about 6 tenths north of it (0.62 km).

**Step 3.** Four-figure reference: **4372**. Six-figure reference: 43 + 1 and 72 + 6 gives **431726**.

visual.alt: Flow of the steps for writing the six-figure reference of the dispensary
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: Let us find the reference of the dispensary. The easting line just to its west is forty three, and the dispensary is about one tenth east of it. The northing line just below it is seventy two, and it is about six tenths above that line. So the four figure reference is four three seven two, and the six figure reference is four three one seven two six.

slides.heading: Quick check: six-figure references
slides.body_md: Build a six-figure reference from easting, northing and tenths.
slides.narration: Quick check. Remember: easting first, then northing, and tenths come from the bottom left corner.

slides.heading: Finding the feature at a reference
slides.body_md: To name the feature at a given reference, reverse the steps: split the number into easting and northing, go to that point, and read the symbol using the key. For **468738**: easting 46 and 8 tenths, northing 73 and 8 tenths gives the **post office** at the edge of Nandiwadi.

visual.alt: Table of four six-figure references on the imagined sheet and the feature found at each
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: To find what lies at a reference, work backwards. Split the six figures into the easting part and the northing part, go to that point on the sheet, and read the symbol using the key. Four six eight seven three eight leads to the post office on the edge of Nandiwadi. Always check that you did not swap the two halves.

slides.heading: Contours and the contour interval
slides.body_md: A **contour** is an imaginary line joining places of **equal height** above mean sea level; on the sheet it is a thin **brown** line. The **contour interval** is the constant difference in height between two neighbouring contours: **20 m** here. Every fifth line is an **index contour** (100 m, 200 m, 300 m, 400 m), drawn thicker and labelled with its height.

visual.alt: Extract of the imagined practice sheet showing closed brown contours rising to a triangulated height of 478 metres on a conical hill
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: A contour is a line joining places of equal height. On our sheet contours are thin brown lines. The difference in height between two neighbouring contours is the contour interval, which is twenty metres here. Every fifth contour is thicker and carries a number. These are the index contours, at one hundred, two hundred, three hundred and four hundred metres.

slides.heading: Worked example: finding the contour interval
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The index contours marked 200 and 300 are the only two numbered lines near a slope. How would you find the contour interval?

**Step 1.** Count the thin lines between them: **4** (they stand for 220, 240, 260, 280 m).

**Step 2.** The gap of 100 m is divided into 4 + 1 = 5 equal intervals.

**Step 3.** Interval = 100 ÷ 5 = **20 m**.

nodes.label: Two index contours: 200 m and 300 m

visual.alt: Flow of the steps for finding the contour interval from two index contours
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: To find the contour interval, take two labelled contours, such as two hundred metres and three hundred metres. Count the thin lines between them. There are four. Four lines make five gaps, so divide the difference of one hundred metres by five. The contour interval is twenty metres.

slides.heading: Quick check: contour interval
slides.body_md: Find the contour interval from two neighbouring contours.
slides.narration: Quick check. The interval is the height difference between two neighbouring contours.

slides.heading: Spacing of contours shows the slope
slides.body_md: **Close** contours mean a **steep** slope (height changes quickly over a short distance). **Widely spaced** contours mean a **gentle** slope. **Evenly spaced** lines mean a uniform slope. You can measure it: average gradient = height difference ÷ distance. On the sheet, the escarpment rises 108 m in 1.3 km (about 83 m per km); the southern plain changes only 40 m in 2.7 km (about 14.8 m per km).

visual.alt: Table comparing the average gradient of the escarpment and the southern plain of the imagined sheet
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: Contours show slope. When the lines are close together the ground rises quickly, so the slope is steep. When they are far apart the ground rises slowly, so the slope is gentle. You can even measure it by dividing the height difference by the distance. On our sheet the escarpment is much steeper than the southern plain.

slides.heading: A cross-section makes the slope visible
slides.body_md: A **cross-section** (profile) is drawn by reading heights along a line. This one runs west to east across the escarpment: the ground is **gentle** at the foot (154 m), **steep** in the middle where the contours are bunched, and **flat** again at the top (262 m). Vertical scale is exaggerated.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Eastings are vertical lines numbered west to east; northings are horizontal lines numbered south to north.
Four-figure reference: easting first, then northing, from the south-west corner of the square.
Six-figure reference: add tenths of the square, easting digits first (temple 463746).
A contour joins equal heights; the contour interval here is 20 m; index contours are every 100 m.
Close contours: steep slope. Wide contours: gentle slope.

rows: Close lines steep, wide lines gentle

visual.alt: Summary table of grid references, contour interval and slope
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Eastings are the vertical lines and northings the horizontal ones. Always read the easting first. Four figures name a square and six figures name a point. A contour joins places of equal height, and the contour interval on our sheet is twenty metres. Close contours mean a steep slope, and wide contours mean a gentle slope.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Write the reference as digits only, with no brackets, and give easting before northing.
Use the lines at the SOUTH-WEST corner of the square; do not read the north-east corner.
Show the count of contours when you work out the interval.
Say "contours are close together" when you explain a steep slope, and name the place.

rows: Along the corridor first, then up the stairs
Reading tenths from the top right
Tenths come from the bottom left
Dividing by the number of lines
Divide by the number of gaps, one more than the lines

visual.alt: Table of three common slips with grid references and contour interval, and their fixes
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: Some tips for the paper. Write only digits in a grid reference, easting first. Use the bottom left corner of the square. When you find the contour interval, count the gaps between contours, not the lines. And when you explain a steep slope, say that the contours are close together and name the place you mean.

decks.title: Topographical Maps: Grid References, Contours and Heights, Part 2: Landforms and heights
goals: Recognise a conical hill, a ridge, an escarpment, and steep and gentle slopes from their contours
Distinguish a triangulated height from a spot height
Calculate relative height and relative depth between two points

slides.heading: Landforms hidden in the contours
slides.body_md: Contours let you see **landforms** on a flat sheet. On our imagined sheet you can find a **conical hill** in the north, a **ridge** in the north-west, an **escarpment** in the east, a **river valley** running south-east and a **gentle plain** in the south and south-west. This part shows how to read each one.

visual.alt: Table of four landforms of the imagined sheet and the squares where they lie
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: Contours turn a flat sheet into a landscape. On our imagined sheet there is a conical hill in the north, a long ridge in the north west, and an escarpment in the east. The south and south west form a gentle plain. In this part we learn to recognise each of these from the pattern of the contours.

slides.heading: Landforms and their contour patterns
slides.body_md: **Conical hill:** closed, roughly circular contours, one inside another, with a summit in the middle. **Ridge:** long, narrow closed contours or a long crest with slopes falling on both sides. **Escarpment:** contours crowded together along a line (a long steep face) with widely spaced lines on one side and a flat top on the other. **Steep slope:** close contours. **Gentle slope:** wide spacing. **Valley:** V-shaped bends pointing to higher ground.

rows: Concentric closed rings, steep on all sides
Elongated closed contours, crest in the middle

visual.alt: Table of landforms and the contour pattern that shows each
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: Here is the code. A conical hill shows as closed rings, one inside another, with the summit in the middle. A ridge is a long narrow set of closed contours. An escarpment is a line along which many contours are crowded together. Close contours are a steep slope, and wide spacing is a gentle slope. A valley shows as bends that point to higher ground.

slides.heading: The conical hill
slides.body_md: The extract shows concentric closed contours around a triangulated height of **478 m** near easting 46, northing 78. Notice how the lines are **evenly crowded on every side**: the slopes are steep in all directions, and the top is small. The 300 m index contour encloses the summit, so the hill rises about 178 m above it.

visual.alt: Extract of the imagined practice sheet showing closed brown contours rising to a triangulated height of 478 metres on a conical hill
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: This is the conical hill. The contours form closed rings, one inside another, round a small summit with a triangulated height of four hundred and seventy eight metres. The rings are close together on every side, so the slopes are steep in all directions. The three hundred metre contour encloses the summit, so the hill rises a further one hundred seventy eight metres above that line.

slides.heading: The ridge
slides.body_md: The ridge in the north-west is a **long, narrow** upland. Its contours are stretched into long loops, and its crest carries a triangulated height of **398 m**. The slopes on the two long sides are steep; the crest is nearly level for about 2 km. Notice that the ridge is **lower** than the conical hill, and that a lower saddle lies between the two.

visual.alt: Extract of the imagined practice sheet showing long, narrow closed contours of a ridge with a triangulated height of 398 metres
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: Now the ridge in the north west. Its contours are stretched into long narrow loops, so the landform is long and narrow rather than round. The crest has a triangulated height of three hundred and ninety eight metres. The two long sides are steep, and the crest is nearly level. It is lower than the conical hill we just studied.

slides.heading: Quick check: recognising a landform
slides.body_md: Name the landform from its contour pattern.
slides.narration: Quick check. Concentric closed rings with a summit in the middle show a conical hill.

slides.heading: The escarpment
slides.body_md: An **escarpment** is a long, steep face that separates a higher flat area from lower ground. On the extract, contours are **bunched** between easting 48 and 49, then **spread out** on the flat top to the east. The foot is at 154 m and the top at 262 m, so the face is about 108 m high.

visual.alt: Extract of the imagined practice sheet showing very closely spaced contours of an escarpment, with spot heights of 154 and 262 metres on either side
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: This is the escarpment in the east. Many contours are bunched together along a line, which shows a long steep face. To the west the ground is gentle, and to the east the top is flat again, with widely spaced lines. The foot is at one hundred and fifty four metres, and the top is at two hundred and sixty two.

slides.heading: Worked example: naming landforms from descriptions
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Name the landform in each description.

**(a)** Closed, nearly circular contours, one inside another, with a triangulated height at the centre. **Conical hill.**

**(b)** Contours bunched along a line for 2 km; to the east they open out at about 260 m. **Escarpment** (steep face and a flat top).

**(c)** Long narrow loops with the highest value in the middle; the slopes on both long sides are steep. **Ridge.**

visual.alt: Table of three contour descriptions with the landform and the reason for each
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: Let us name some landforms. Closed circular contours, one inside another, with a triangulated height at the centre, show a conical hill. Contours bunched along a line, with wide spacing beyond, show an escarpment. Long narrow loops with the highest value in the middle show a ridge. Always give the reason along with the name.

slides.heading: Quick check: ridge or escarpment
slides.body_md: Tell a ridge from an escarpment.
slides.narration: Quick check. A ridge has steep sides on both long edges; an escarpment is steep on one side only.

slides.heading: Reading the hill from a cross-section
slides.body_md: The cross-section runs south to north along easting 46.05 over the conical hill. Heights climb from about 180 m at northing 76 to the summit of **478 m** at northing 78.45 and fall again. The **steepest** stretches are the flanks where contours crowd; near the top the ground flattens.

slides.heading: Triangulated heights and spot heights
slides.body_md: A **triangulated height** (black triangle with a figure) is a point fixed by the survey's triangulation network on a **summit or prominent point**; it is the most accurate height. A **spot height** (black dot with a figure) is a height measured at an ordinary place, such as a road junction or a plain, to fill gaps between contours. Both give height in **metres above mean sea level**. The summit triangle here reads 478; spot heights read 154, 262 and others.

slides.heading: Worked example: relative height of the escarpment
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the relative height of the escarpment from the spot heights at its top (262 m, reference 491755) and its foot (154 m, reference 478755).

**Step 1.** Higher point: 262 m. Lower point: 154 m.

**Step 2.** Relative height = 262 − 154 = **108 m**.

So the top is 108 m higher than the foot; the foot is 108 m lower than the top (a relative **depth** if you look from the top).

The spot height at the top of the escarpment is two hundred and sixty two metres, and at the foot it is one hundred and fifty four. slides.heading: Relative height and relative depth
slides.body_md: **Relative height** = height of the higher point − height of the lower point. **Relative depth** is the same difference, measured downwards from the higher point (for example the depth of a valley below a ridge). Never add the two heights. Example: the summit (478 m) stands 326 m above the temple, whose ground height is 152 m.

notes.title: Topographical Maps: Grid References, Contours and Heights: Notes

sections.heading: 1. The sheet and its grid
sections.body_md:
- A **topographical sheet** is a large-scale map of a small area showing relief, drainage, settlements, communications and land use.
- The ICSE paper uses a real Survey of India sheet. These notes use an **imagined practice sheet** (not a real place, not a Survey of India sheet).
- **Eastings** are the vertical grid lines, numbered west to east along the top and bottom (here 40 to 50).
- **Northings** are the horizontal grid lines, numbered south to north along the sides (here 70 to 80).
- Each grid square is 1 km by 1 km (1 sq km); at 1 cm to 0.5 km it measures 2 cm by 2 cm on the printed sheet.

key_terms.definition_md: A vertical grid line; its number increases towards the east.
A horizontal grid line; its number increases towards the north.

visual.alt: Table of the grid of the imagined sheet
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet

sections.heading: 2. Four-figure and six-figure grid references
sections.body_md:
- **Four-figure reference** (a square): **easting first, then northing**, taken from the lines at the **south-west corner** of the square. The temple is in square **4674**.
- **Six-figure reference** (a point): easting (2 digits) + tenths eastwards, northing (2 digits) + tenths northwards. The temple is **463746**, the post office **468738** and the dispensary **431726**.
- To find the feature at a reference, split it into the easting half and the northing half, go to that point and read the symbol with the key.

key_terms.definition_md: Two digits for the easting then two for the northing; names a whole 1 km square.
Adds a tenth digit to each half; names a point to the nearest 0.1 km.

visual.alt: Table of grid references of three features of the imagined sheet
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet

sections.heading: 3. Contours and the contour interval
sections.body_md:
- A **contour** is a line joining places of equal height above mean sea level (brown on the sheet).
- The **contour interval** is the constant height difference between neighbouring contours: **20 m** on the imagined sheet.
- **Index contours** (every 100 m here) are thicker and labelled.
- Finding the interval: height difference between two labelled contours divided by the number of **gaps** (lines between + 1).
- Heights between contours: a point between the 160 m and 180 m contours has a height between 160 m and 180 m.

key_terms.definition_md: The constant difference in height between two neighbouring contours.
Every fifth contour, drawn thicker and labelled with its height.

visual.alt: Table showing the contour interval worked out from two index contours
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet

sections.heading: 4. Slope from contour spacing
sections.body_md:
- **Close** contours: **steep** slope. **Wide** spacing: **gentle** slope. **Even** spacing: uniform slope.
- Average gradient = height difference ÷ horizontal distance.
- On the imagined sheet the escarpment rises 108 m in about 1.3 km (about 83 m per km); the southern plain changes about 14.8 m per km.
- A **cross-section** drawn from the heights along a line shows the slope as a profile.

key_terms.definition_md: Height difference divided by horizontal distance, for example in metres per km.
A profile drawn from the heights along a chosen line.

visual.alt: Table linking contour spacing to slope
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet

sections.heading: 5. Landforms from contours
sections.body_md:
- **Conical hill:** concentric closed contours, steep on all sides, small summit (478 m here).
- **Ridge:** long narrow closed contours with a crest (398 m here), steep on both long sides.
- **Escarpment:** contours bunched along a line (the steep face) with wide spacing on one side and a flat top on the other.
- **Steep slope** and **gentle slope** follow the spacing; a **valley** shows V-shaped bends pointing to higher ground.
- Sketch each by drawing the contours and labelling the highest value.

key_terms.definition_md: A hill with steep slopes on all sides shown by concentric closed contours.
A long steep face between a higher flat area and lower ground.
A long narrow upland with a crest and slopes falling on both sides.

visual.alt: Table of three landforms and their contour patterns
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet

sections.heading: 6. Triangulated heights, spot heights and relative height
sections.body_md:
- **Triangulated height:** black triangle with a figure, fixed by survey triangulation on a summit or prominent point (478 m on the hill, 398 m on the ridge).
- **Spot height:** black dot with a figure, measured at ordinary ground to fill gaps between contours.
- Both are in metres above mean sea level.
- **Relative height** = higher height − lower height (for example 262 m − 154 m = 108 m for the escarpment). **Relative depth** is the same difference measured downwards.
- Never add the two heights.

key_terms.definition_md: A height fixed by a survey network and marked by a black triangle on a summit or prominent point.
A height of an ordinary point, marked by a black dot and a figure.
The difference in height between two points.

visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing the northing before the easting.
- Reading tenths from the top right instead of the south-west corner.
- Dividing by the number of lines instead of the number of gaps when finding the contour interval.
- Adding two heights instead of subtracting for relative height.
- Calling a ridge a hill, or forgetting units.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Grid reference (1 mark each): correct digits in the right order.
- Contour interval or height (1 to 2 marks): value with the unit and the working.
- Landform (2 marks): the name and the contour evidence.

cards.front_md: Define contour interval.
cards.back_md: The constant height difference between neighbouring contours.

cards.front_md: Contour interval of the imagined sheet?
How often are index contours drawn here?
cards.back_md: Every 100 m (every fifth contour); thicker and labelled.

cards.front_md: Contour interval from two labelled contours?
cards.back_md: Height difference divided by the number of gaps (lines between + 1).

cards.front_md: What do close contours show?
cards.back_md: A steep slope.

cards.front_md: What do widely spaced contours show?
cards.back_md: A gentle slope.

cards.front_md: Average gradient formula?
cards.back_md: Height difference ÷ horizontal distance.

cards.front_md: Contour pattern of a conical hill?
cards.back_md: Concentric closed contours, steep on all sides.

cards.front_md: Contour pattern of a ridge?
cards.back_md: Long narrow closed contours with a crest in the middle.

cards.front_md: Contour pattern of an escarpment?
cards.back_md: Contours bunched along a line, wide spacing beyond (steep face, flat top).

cards.front_md: V-shaped contour bends point to?
cards.back_md: Higher ground (a valley).

cards.front_md: Symbol of a triangulated height?
cards.back_md: A black triangle with a figure.

cards.front_md: Symbol of a spot height?
cards.back_md: A black dot with a figure.

cards.front_md: Relative height formula?
cards.back_md: Higher height minus lower height.

cards.front_md: Relative height of the escarpment on the imagined sheet?
Heights on a sheet are measured above?
cards.back_md: Mean sea level.

questions.stem_md: On the imagined practice sheet, which of these contours is an index contour (thicker and labelled)?
questions.solution_md: Index contours are drawn every 100 m, so 300 m is an index contour — option (b).

questions.stem_md: On the imagined practice sheet the 200 m and 300 m index contours have four thin contours between them. Calculate the contour interval in metres.
questions.solution_md: The four thin contours make 5 equal gaps. Interval = 100 ÷ 5 = 20 m.

questions.stem_md: On another sheet, 3 thin contours lie between a 100 m and a 200 m index contour. The contour interval on that sheet is ___ m.
questions.solution_md: Three lines make 4 gaps: 100 ÷ 4 = **25** m.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The height difference between one contour and the next is the same everywhere on a sheet.
questions.solution_md: True: it is the contour interval (20 m on the imagined sheet).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Every point on one contour line has the same height above mean sea level.

**Reason (R):** The height difference between a contour and the next contour is different in different parts of the sheet.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: the contour interval is constant — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the extract, the contours are crowded together between easting 48 and easting 49. This shows that the ground there:
questions.solution_md: Close contours mean a steep slope — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Where the contours on a sheet are far apart, the slope of the ground is:
questions.solution_md: Wide spacing means a gentle slope — option (b).

questions.stem_md: On the imagined practice sheet the spot heights at the foot (154 m) and at the top (262 m) of the escarpment are 1.3 km apart. Calculate the average gradient between them in metres per km, to the nearest whole number.
questions.solution_md: Height difference = 262 − 154 = 108 m. Gradient = 108 ÷ 1.3 = 83 m per km.

questions.stem_md: Study the extract and the cross-section of the south-west of the imagined practice sheet. Describe the slope of the land and give the evidence from the contours.

answer.model_answer_md: The land slopes gently. The contours are few and widely spaced (about 20 m of height over each kilometre or more), and the cross-section changes by only a few tens of metres across three kilometres.

questions.solution_md: Gentle slope; contours wide apart.

A ridge is a river; an escarpment is a hill

questions.stem_md: Why do the contours round a conical hill form closed rings? Give a geographical reason.

answer.model_answer_md: Each contour joins points of the same height, and a hill falls away in every direction from its summit, so every contour must return on itself to enclose the summit.

questions.solution_md: Contours join equal heights and the land falls away in all directions.

marking_scheme.step: Land falls in all directions from the summit
